opus-5.5.text:
I think science is actually one of the most natural places for collaboration, and it's something I feel quite strongly about. If you look at what we did with AlphaFold, we predicted the structures of essentially all the proteins known to science, around 200 million, and we put them in a free database with the European Bioinformatics Institute. Over two million researchers around the world have used it now. That's the model I'd love to see more of: the fruits of these systems going out to the whole scientific community as a kind of root node that unlocks everything downstream.

Science is also less zero-sum than a lot of the commercial competition between labs. Curing diseases, understanding new materials, getting a handle on fusion or climate: these are problems for all of humanity, and nobody benefits from them being solved slowly. So I think there's real room for the labs to share datasets, benchmarks, and in some cases tools, and to work with academia and with the institutions that have decades of domain expertise. The AI people often don't know which questions matter most in biology or chemistry, and the domain experts don't always know what the new techniques can do. The magic happens in that interdisciplinary space, which has always been how I've tried to set things up.

There's a safety angle too. If we can show the world concrete, beneficial applications, things like drug discovery through Isomorphic, or better understanding of disease, then we also build the trust and the norms of working together that we'll need as these systems get more powerful. Collaborating on science is a good rehearsal for collaborating on the harder questions around AGI, like evaluations, safety standards, and making sure the benefits are shared widely. So my hope is that science becomes a kind of common ground, where even fierce competitors can agree that some things are bigger than any one lab.

r001.rationale: The response says science is a natural place for AI labs to collaborate and that shared scientific challenges are less zero-sum than commercial competition, making them common ground.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think science is actually the natural meeting ground for the field, in a way that's perhaps underappreciated. If you look at where the labs compete most fiercely, it's on products, on consumer assistants, on enterprise deals. That's a commercial race and I understand why it looks the way it does. But science is different. Nobody owns the structure of a protein. Nobody owns a better understanding of plasma physics or a new antibiotic. These are public goods, and the benefits accrue to everyone, including the labs themselves.

So when we released the AlphaFold predictions for essentially every known protein, we made them freely available, and now over two million researchers have used that database. That's not something we did despite being a company, it's something we did because we believed the knowledge should be open and that the field advances faster that way. And I'd love to see more of that across the ecosystem. If one lab makes progress on, say, modelling the weather, or on mathematical reasoning, or on materials discovery, the right thing to do is to share the scientific results in the normal way, through publication and open datasets, so others can build on them.

There's also a more practical argument. Science gives us shared benchmarks that actually matter. It's very hard to game whether you've found a real new material that works in the lab, or whether a protein structure is correct. Nature is the ultimate referee. So scientific problems are a place where the labs can calibrate against each other honestly, and where progress is verifiable rather than just a matter of marketing. That's healthy for the whole field, and it's healthy for public trust too.

And then finally, I think it's a safety matter as well. These systems are going to be enormously powerful, and I've always said that one of the most important things we can do is to apply them to problems that are unambiguously good for humanity, like curing diseases or helping with the climate crisis. If the labs collaborate on that, it builds the kind of relationships and shared norms you'd want to have in place when the harder questions come, about how to handle very capable systems responsibly. Science is where we can learn to cooperate before the stakes are at their highest.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts fierce competition over commercial products with science as a shared, public-good domain, and says labs can collaborate on scientific problems and learn to cooperate there.

astra-6.text:
I think science is one of the most promising areas for collaboration, because there are so many fundamental questions where progress benefits everyone. Understanding disease, discovering new materials, tackling energy problems—these are challenges that are much bigger than any one lab.

And there’s a natural complementarity. AI researchers can build powerful models, but scientists bring deep knowledge of the problem, the experimental methods, and the ability to test whether a prediction actually holds up. That feedback is essential. You want a cycle where models help suggest experiments, experiments generate new evidence, and that evidence improves the models.

AI labs can also collaborate on the foundations: shared benchmarks, scientific datasets, and ways to evaluate whether a system is producing reliable, reproducible results. We can compete on approaches while still contributing to a common body of knowledge.

The exciting thing for me is that science gives us something concrete to aim at. It’s not just whether a system sounds intelligent. Has it helped us understand something about the world that we didn’t understand before?

r001.rationale: The response says fundamental scientific questions make science a promising area for collaboration because progress benefits everyone and the challenges exceed any one lab.

sol-6.1.text:
I think science is one of the most exciting opportunities for collaboration, because you have these shared goals that are bigger than any individual lab. Understanding disease, discovering new materials, tackling energy problems—there’s an enormous amount of work to do, and success benefits everybody.

And the AI is only one part of it. You need the expertise of scientists who understand the problem deeply, and you need experiments to test whether the predictions actually hold up. That creates a very natural partnership between AI labs, universities, and experimental groups.

I’d love to see more collaboration around concrete scientific challenges, where we can share tools and evaluate progress against something real. Does this help us understand nature better? Does it lead to a useful discovery? I think that’s a wonderful common purpose for the field.

r001.rationale: It presents major scientific challenges as shared goals bigger than any one lab and calls collaboration around them a natural partnership and common purpose.
